name: Gasa
tagline: Hot springs and a frontier dzong at the top of the Mo Chhu
meta_description: Gasa, Bhutan: Gasa Tsachu hot springs, Gasa Dzong, Jigme Dorji National Park, the road from Punakha, Laya and the Royal Highlander Festival, and 2026 costs.
summary: Gasa is Bhutan's smallest and least populated district town, at about 2,800 m in the far north, 3–4 hours up the Mo Chhu valley from Punakha. Come for Gasa Tsachu, the hot springs Bhutanese families visit in winter, the frontier dzong, and as the road head for Laya and Jigme Dorji National Park.
intro: Most travellers go no further north than Punakha Dzong. Follow the Mo Chhu upstream from there, though, and the road climbs for 3–4 hours through rice terraces, then forest, into the high, steep valleys of Gasa. The district is the least populated in Bhutan, and most of it lies inside Jigme Dorji National Park, which runs up to the border with Tibet. The town itself is tiny: a dzong, district offices, a school, a few shops and houses strung along the slope at about 2,800 m.

Bhutanese know Gasa for one thing above all: the tsachu, the hot springs below the town. Every winter, families and groups of pilgrims come for days or weeks at a time to bathe in the pools, which are believed to ease aches and illnesses. The government has rebuilt the bathing area with covered pools at different temperatures, changing rooms and simple places to stay. For visitors, a soak here is one of the most local things you can do in Bhutan, and you will usually be the only tourists in the water.

Gasa is also the start of some of Bhutan's great treks. The trail to Laya, a high village of yak herders at about 3,800 m, begins here, and the long Snowman Trek passes through. Since 2017, Laya has hosted the Royal Highlander Festival in October, which brings herders from across the north. Gasa needs a route permit, which your operator arranges in Thimphu, and a licensed guide. The road from Punakha can be damaged by landslides in the monsoon; check current status before you travel.

story.title: A dzong on the northern frontier
paras: Gasa Dzong, formally Tashi Thongmoen Dzong, stands on a hill above the town with snow peaks behind it on clear days. It was built in the 17th century under Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, the founder of the Bhutanese state, when Tibetan armies were repeatedly attacking the young country from the north. Gasa sat on one of the routes over the mountains from Tibet, and the dzong was built to watch and defend it. Its round shape, with buildings arranged around a central tower, is unusual among Bhutan's dzongs.

For centuries Gasa was also a trading post. Herders from Laya and Lunana, the high villages to the north, brought yak products, cheese and butter down to exchange for rice and other goods from the Punakha valley. Before the road came, the walk from Punakha took several days, and the Gasa route was one of the main links between the high north and the rest of Bhutan.

The hot springs have their own place in tradition. Bhutanese believe the waters of a tsachu carry healing power, and local accounts link the Gasa springs to blessings from great lamas of the past. Whatever you believe, the bathing season tells the story: in December, January and February, the pools fill with farmers, monks and families who come after the harvest to rest, talk and soak for days.
story.source: Gasa District, Gasa Dzong and Jigme Dorji National Park articles (Wikipedia); Gasa Dzongkhag Administration; Department of Tourism, Bhutan

did_you_know: Gasa is the least populated of Bhutan's 20 districts.
Most of Gasa District lies within Jigme Dorji National Park, which stretches north to the border with Tibet.
The Royal Highlander Festival, celebrating Bhutan's high-altitude herders, has been held at Laya in Gasa District since 2017.

highlights.title: Gasa Tsachu hot springs
highlights.text: Covered bathing pools fed by hot springs, each at a different temperature, used by Bhutanese families and pilgrims for days at a time in winter. Bring a swimsuit and towel, follow local etiquette, and plan an evening and a morning soak.

highlights.title: Gasa Dzong
highlights.text: A 17th-century frontier dzong on a hill above town, built under the Zhabdrung to guard the route from Tibet. Its rounded plan around a central tower is unusual. On clear days snow peaks rise behind it, best seen in the morning.

highlights.title: The drive up the Mo Chhu
highlights.text: The road from Punakha follows the Mo Chhu north past rice terraces, farm villages and the turn to Tashithang, then climbs through forest. It is slow but scenic, and you see a side of Bhutan most visitors miss.

highlights.title: Jigme Dorji National Park
highlights.text: Bhutan's second-largest protected area covers most of the district, from subtropical forest to glaciers. It is home to takin, blue sheep and snow leopards, though you are unlikely to see the rarer animals on a short visit.

highlights.title: Gateway to Laya
highlights.text: Gasa is the road head for treks to Laya, a high village of yak herders known for the women's conical bamboo hats. The Royal Highlander Festival takes place there in October. Reaching Laya needs extra days and careful planning.

how_to_reach.text: From Punakha, the road runs north along the Mo Chhu and climbs to Gasa, about 70–80 km and 3–4 hours depending on road conditions. Some stretches are narrow and rough. A Bhutan-registered car with driver costs about ₹4,500–6,500 a day, indicative 2026; ask your operator whether a 4WD is advised. Landslides close the road at times in the monsoon; check current status before you travel.

Gasa is outside the Thimphu–Paro area, so your operator gets a route permit from the immigration office in Thimphu on a working day. A licensed guide is required for both Indian and international visitors, and treks to Laya need a trekking permit and a licensed trekking guide. Check current status before you travel.

The nearest airport is Paro, about 6–7 hours by road via Thimphu and Punakha. Overland, enter at Phuentsholing via NJP or Hasimara and reach Punakha over two days. Most travellers go to Gasa from a base in Punakha.

where_to_stay: Gasa has very few places for tourists. Around the hot springs there are simple government-built guesthouses and rooms used mainly by Bhutanese bathers, with basic bathrooms and shared facilities; ask your operator what is currently certified for tourists. In the town itself there are one or two small guesthouses. Many visitors instead stay in the Punakha valley, at Hotel Lobesa or Dhensa Boutique Resort, and do Gasa as a long day trip, but that leaves only an hour or two in the water. If you want a proper soak, take a night at Gasa with low expectations of the room.
costs: Free or a small fee, check current status before you travel
Simple guesthouse room near the springs
₹1,200 / US$100 per person per night, check current status before you travel
budget_tip: Pair a Gasa night with your Punakha stay instead of adding a separate leg; you keep the same car and guide and only add one night of SDF and a simple room.
tips: Bring a swimsuit, towel and flip-flops for the hot springs; bathing naked is not the custom in the shared pools.
Do not soak for too long at a time in the hottest pools, and drink water; the heat and altitude combine.
Carry cash in small notes and snacks; shops in Gasa are few and simple.
Avoid June to August: the road from Punakha is prone to landslides and the views are hidden in cloud.
Dress warmly for evenings; Gasa at 2,800 m is near freezing at night from November to March.

experiences.title: A soak in Gasa Tsachu
experiences.best_time: Dec–Feb for the local bathing season; Oct–Apr generally
experiences.cost: Free or a small fee, check current status before you travel
experiences.summary: Bathe in the covered hot spring pools below Gasa town alongside Bhutanese families and pilgrims. Each pool has a different temperature, and in winter people stay for days. It is one of the most local experiences open to visitors in Bhutan.
body: Gasa Tsachu lies below the town, near the river, where hot water rises from the ground. The springs have been used for generations, and the government has rebuilt the bathing area with several covered pools, changing rooms and nearby lodging. Each pool is fed by a different spring and has its own temperature, from warm to very hot. Bhutanese believe that different springs help different ailments, and you will see people moving between pools with purpose.

The busy season is winter, especially December to February, after the harvest. Families arrive with bedding, food and cooking pots and stay in the lodges for a week or more, bathing several times a day. The pools then become social places, full of talk and laughter. In spring and autumn they are quieter. For visitors, an evening soak and another at dawn is ideal, which means staying a night.

Bring a swimsuit and towel; locals bathe in shorts or wrapped in cloth, and full nakedness is not the custom in mixed or shared pools. Shower or rinse before getting in, do not use soap or shampoo in the pools, and keep your voice down. Do not stay too long in the hottest pool, drink water, and get out if you feel dizzy. People with heart conditions should take medical advice before using very hot pools.

faqs.q: Can tourists use Gasa hot springs
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors with a route permit and a licensed guide can bathe in the Gasa Tsachu pools alongside Bhutanese families. Bring a swimsuit and towel, rinse before entering, and do not use soap in the pools. Entry is free or a small fee. Ask your guide which pools are open and their temperatures. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Gasa Tsachu
faqs.a: December to February is the traditional bathing season, when Bhutanese families come after the harvest and stay for days; it is lively and cold. October, November, March and April are quieter and the road is usually good. Avoid June to August, when landslides can close the road from Punakha. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are the Gasa hot springs safe
faqs.a: For healthy adults, yes, if you use common sense. Some pools are very hot. Test the water first, limit each soak to 10–20 minutes, drink water, and get out if you feel dizzy or faint. Pregnant women, young children and people with heart or blood pressure problems should take medical advice before using the hottest pools.

experiences.title: Gasa Dzong on the northern frontier
experiences.cost: Free or a small fee, check current status before you travel
experiences.summary: A visit to the 17th-century dzong above Gasa town, built under the Zhabdrung to guard the northern route from Tibet. Its rounded plan is unusual, and on clear mornings snow peaks rise behind it.
body: Gasa Dzong, formally called Tashi Thongmoen Dzong, stands on a hill overlooking the town and the valley. It was built in the 17th century under Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, when the new Bhutanese state was defending itself against Tibetan attacks from the north, and Gasa sat on one of the routes across the mountains. Like other dzongs, it now holds both the district administration and a monk body.

The dzong's layout is rounded, with buildings and walls arranged around a central tower, instead of the long rectangles of Punakha or Paro. It is smaller than the great dzongs of the west, and much less visited. With your guide you can see the courtyard and, when open, the main temple. On clear mornings, look north beyond it for snow peaks on the edge of Jigme Dorji National Park.

Combine the dzong with a soak at the hot springs on the same visit. Usual rules apply: long sleeves, long trousers or a skirt, no caps inside, and no photographs in the temples. Timings depend on office hours and religious work, so let your guide check on the day.

faqs.q: How old is Gasa Dzong
faqs.a: Gasa Dzong was built in the 17th century under Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, as a defence on Bhutan's northern frontier at a time of repeated Tibetan attacks. It has been repaired and renovated since. Today it houses Gasa's district administration and a monk body, like other dzongs in Bhutan, and visitors can enter with a licensed guide.

faqs.q: Is Gasa Dzong worth the drive
faqs.a: On its own, probably not for a short trip, as it is 3–4 hours from Punakha. Combined with a night at the Gasa hot springs, yes: you get a quiet frontier dzong with mountain views, a local bathing experience and the drive up the Mo Chhu valley, all without crowds.

faqs.q: What is special about Gasa Dzong's design
faqs.a: Most Bhutanese dzongs are long and rectangular, built around one or more courtyards. Gasa Dzong is rounded, with buildings and walls arranged around a central tower, and sits on a hilltop that gave its guards a view over the approach from the north. It is smaller and more compact than the great dzongs of Punakha, Paro or Trongsa.

experiences.title: The Royal Highlander Festival at Laya
experiences.cost: Festival free; trek or transport and guide extra, indicative
experiences.image_query: Laya Bhutan Layap women bamboo hat
experiences.summary: A festival of Bhutan's high-altitude herders, held at Laya in Gasa District each October since 2017, with yaks, horses, highland dress, songs and competitions. Getting there takes extra days and planning.
body: Laya is a village of yak herders at about 3,800 m in the far north of Gasa District, below the snow peaks along the Tibet border. The Layaps have their own dress, and the women's conical bamboo hats, topped with a spike, are among the best-known images of highland Bhutan. Since 2017, Laya has hosted the Royal Highlander Festival every October, bringing herders from Laya, Lunana and other high communities together with their animals.

The festival includes yak and horse displays, highland songs and dances, traditional games, displays of local products and cultural programmes. Exact dates and programmes are announced each year, and in some years the festival has been changed or not held, so plan only once dates are confirmed. Accommodation is mostly in tents and simple village homes.

Getting to Laya takes time. Depending on how far the road reaches in your year, it is a trek of one or two days from the road head beyond Gasa, climbing steadily through forest along the Mo Chhu. You need a trekking permit, a licensed trekking guide, warm gear and good fitness. Budget at least 5–6 days from Punakha. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Royal Highlander Festival
faqs.a: It has been held at Laya in Gasa District in October each year since 2017, usually over two days. Dates and programmes are announced annually and can change, and the festival has not been held in every year. Ask your operator for the confirmed dates before planning, as the trip to Laya takes several days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do you get to Laya
faqs.a: Drive from Punakha to Gasa and beyond to the current road head, then trek for one or two days along the Mo Chhu to Laya at about 3,800 m. You need a trekking permit, a licensed trekking guide and camping or village homestay arrangements through your operator. Allow 5–6 days for the round trip from Punakha. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Who are the Layaps
faqs.a: The Layaps are the yak-herding people of Laya in northern Gasa District. They have their own dialect and dress, and Layap women are known for their conical bamboo hats with a spike on top. Their livelihood has traditionally depended on yaks and, in recent decades, the seasonal collection of cordyceps on the high pastures.

experiences.title: A forest walk in Jigme Dorji National Park
experiences.cost: Free; guide as part of your day rate
experiences.image_query: Jigme Dorji National Park Bhutan forest
experiences.summary: An easy guided walk on village and forest trails around Gasa, inside Jigme Dorji National Park, Bhutan's second-largest protected area. Expect old forest, birds, farm villages and long views, rather than rare animal sightings.
body: Jigme Dorji National Park covers most of Gasa District and parts of the neighbouring districts, from warm broadleaf forest in the south to alpine meadows and glaciers on the Tibet border. It is Bhutan's second-largest protected area and is home to takin, Bhutan's national animal, as well as blue sheep, red panda, Himalayan black bear and snow leopard. Several of Bhutan's important rivers, including the Mo Chhu, rise inside it.

Around Gasa, your guide can take you on village paths and forest trails for a few hours: down towards the hot springs, along farm tracks between houses and fields, or into mixed forest of oak, rhododendron and conifer. Spring brings rhododendron flowers and more birdsong; October and November have clearer views of the snow peaks. You are unlikely to see the rarer mammals, which keep to remote areas, but birding can be good.

Walk with your guide, keep to paths, and do not pick plants; the park protects many medicinal and rare species. Carry water, snacks and a warm layer, as the weather changes quickly. Combine a morning walk with a soak in the hot springs in the afternoon for a full Gasa day.

faqs.q: Can you see takin in Jigme Dorji National Park
faqs.a: Takin live in the park, especially in the higher valleys in summer, but sightings on a short walk around Gasa are unlikely. For a sure sighting, visit the Motithang Takin Preserve in Thimphu. In the park, birds, flowers and forest are the main attractions on a day walk, with distant snow peaks on clear days.

faqs.q: How big is Jigme Dorji National Park
faqs.a: It covers about 4,300 sq km across Gasa and parts of neighbouring districts, which makes it Bhutan's second-largest protected area after Wangchuck Centennial National Park. It runs from subtropical forest in the south to glaciers and high peaks on the Tibet border, and includes the high villages of Laya and Lingzhi.

faqs.q: Do I need a special permit to walk in the park
faqs.a: For short walks around Gasa with your licensed guide, your route permit for Gasa is usually enough. Multi-day treks inside the park need a trekking permit and a licensed trekking guide, arranged through your operator. Some park fees may apply on treks. Check current status before you travel, as rules are revised from time to time.

faqs.q: How far is Gasa from Punakha
faqs.a: About 70–80 km, or 3–4 hours by car, following the Mo Chhu north from Punakha and climbing through forest to Gasa at about 2,800 m. Some stretches are narrow and rough, and monsoon landslides can close the road. Most visitors go from a base in Punakha and stay one night at Gasa. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Gasa worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, for travellers who have seen the main western sights and want something local and quiet. The hot springs, a small frontier dzong and the drive up the Mo Chhu valley are the reasons to go. On a first short trip to Bhutan, Punakha and Phobjikha are better uses of the time.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Gasa
faqs.a: Yes. Gasa is outside the Thimphu–Paro area covered by the entry permit, so your operator needs a route permit from the immigration office in Thimphu, issued on working days. A licensed guide is required. Treks beyond Gasa to Laya need a separate trekking permit and a licensed trekking guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do Gasa as a day trip from Punakha
faqs.a: It is possible but long: 6–8 hours of driving in total, leaving only an hour or two at the hot springs and the dzong. We suggest one night at Gasa so you can soak in the evening and the morning. If time is short, do the drive only if the road is in good condition.

faqs.q: Is Gasa the least populated district in Bhutan
faqs.a: Yes. Gasa is the least populated of Bhutan's 20 districts, with only a few thousand residents spread across a large, mountainous area, most of it inside Jigme Dorji National Park. Haa is the second least populated. Settlements include Gasa town, Laya and Lunana, the last two among the highest villages in the country.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Gasa
faqs.a: Gasa at about 2,800 m is cool most of the year. Winter days can be sunny and around 5–12 °C, with nights near or below freezing. Spring and autumn are mild. June to August is the monsoon, with heavy rain, cloud and landslide risk on the road. October to April is the best time to visit.

faqs.q: What should I bring to the Gasa hot springs
faqs.a: A swimsuit or shorts and T-shirt, a quick-dry towel, flip-flops, a warm jacket for walking between pools and lodgings, a water bottle and a small bag for wet clothes. Bring your own toiletries for showering, but do not use soap or shampoo in the pools. A head torch helps for evening soaks.

faqs.q: Can I trek from Gasa to Laya
faqs.a: Yes, with a licensed operator and trekking guide. The route follows the Mo Chhu north from the road head beyond Gasa to Laya, about 3,800 m, over one or two days depending on how far the road reaches. It needs fitness, warm gear and acclimatisation. Laya is also on the longer Laya–Gasa and Snowman trek routes.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for Gasa
faqs.a: Simple government-built guesthouses near the hot springs and one or two small places in town are the only options, mostly basic. Ask your operator which are certified for tourists. Many travellers stay in the Punakha valley at Hotel Lobesa or Dhensa Boutique Resort and visit Gasa for a day or one night only.
